summary: A one-chapter sermon disguised as a letter: Jeremiah writes to the exiles being carried to Babylon — 'ye shall remain there many years, and for a long season, namely, seven generations' — to warn them about the gods they are about to see. What follows is a sustained, often darkly funny demolition: gods gilded by workmen, gods the priests rob, gods that cannot see the dust on their own faces, gods carried on shoulders, gods rusting, gods that are 'as a scarecrow in a garden of cucumbers.' The refrain repeats like a hammer: 'they are no gods: therefore fear them not.' It ends: 'Better therefore is the just man that hath no idols.'
whyItMatters: This is the Bible's longest sustained satire of idolatry — a survival manual for believers living in an idol-saturated culture. Its logic is simple and devastating: anything that cannot save itself is not a savior. Every generation of exiles — including ours — has needed the letter.

context.author: Anonymous, writing under Jeremiah's name (pseudepigraphic); the historical Jeremiah wrote a letter to the exiles (Jeremiah 29)
context.audience: Jewish exiles in Babylon — and every community since that lives among idols
context.date: Composed in the Greek period (2nd century BC or so); set at the exile's beginning (597 BC)
context.setting: Jerusalem, writing to Babylon — the letter travels with the deportees

outline.heading: The letter's frame
outline.note: Sent ahead of the captives; seven generations in Babylon

outline.heading: The warning
outline.note: You will see gods of silver, gold, and wood — 'say ye in your hearts, O Lord, we must worship thee'

outline.heading: The catalog of absurdities
outline.note: Gilded, robbed, dusty, bat-perched, door-locked, fire-burned gods

outline.heading: The true powers by contrast
outline.note: Sun, moon, stars, lightning, wind, clouds, fire — obedient to God

outline.heading: The conclusion
outline.note: Better a king, a vessel, a door, a pillar — better the just man without idols

keyVerses.text: Beware therefore that ye in no wise be like to strangers, neither be ye afraid of them, when ye see the multitude before them and behind them, worshipping them. But say ye in your hearts, O Lord, we must worship thee.
keyVerses.why: The letter's practical program: the crowd's worship is contagious — the counter is a sentence kept in the heart.

keyVerses.text: Whereby they are known not to be gods: therefore fear them not.
keyVerses.why: The refrain's logic — divinity is tested by power to save; gods that cannot save themselves fail the test.

keyVerses.text: For as a scarecrow in a garden of cucumbers keepeth nothing: so are their gods of wood, and laid over with silver and gold.
keyVerses.why: The letter's most famous image — a god as effective as a scarecrow: dressed up, feared by no one who thinks.

keyVerses.text: Better therefore is the just man that hath no idols: for he shall be far from reproach.
keyVerses.why: The conclusion flips the comparison: not just 'idols are worse than useful things' — the person without idols outranks them all.

themes: The test of power to save

questions.question: Why is this a separate book here but part of Baruch in Catholic Bibles?
questions.answer: The Greek Septuagint transmits it as an independent scroll; the Latin Vulgate attached it to Baruch as a sixth chapter, and Catholic Bibles follow the Vulgate. Orthodox Bibles (following the Septuagint) keep it separate — as this arrangement does. Same letter, two shelving decisions.

questions.question: Did Jeremiah really write it?
questions.answer: Almost certainly not — the style, Greek language, and situation point to a later Jewish author writing 'in the spirit' of Jeremiah, whose letter to the exiles (Jeremiah 29) it deliberately echoes. Ancient readers accepted such authorized ventriloquism as a literary form; modern readers should know the genre for what it is.

questions.question: Why 'seven generations' in Babylon?
questions.answer: It echoes Jeremiah 29's seventy years — roughly a lifetime of three to four generations stretched to seven for emphasis. The number tells the exiles: do not plan to assimilate and go home soon; build a durable faith for the long stay.

questions.question: Is the satire disrespectful, or is it theology?
questions.answer: Both — deliberately. The letter's method is reductio: list what the gods actually do (rust, dust, bats, theft, fire) and let the absurdity argue. Behind the mockery stands serious theology: divinity is known by power to save (1:36-37), and the true powers — sun, stars, wind — obey God's command (1:60-62).

questions.question: What are the modern idols this letter would name?
questions.answer: The letter's test transfers directly: anything you serve that cannot save itself — money that fails in a crash, systems that rust, reputations that moths eat, powers that need locks and guards. The exiles' danger was not statues as such but the fear that keeps a community bowing. 'Say ye in your hearts, O Lord, we must worship thee' is the letter's whole alternative.
